head:
Health · Cardio

Cardio and lifespan: what the data show, and what they do not show

Your doctor measures your blood pressure, your weight, sometimes your cholesterol. Almost never your endurance. Yet, across hundreds of thousands of people, it is one of the measures that says the most about what comes next. This article follows a single question, from the broadest to the most precise, all the way to its limits: does your endurance say anything about how long you will live, and does working on it change anything?

The problem

“Cardio is good for your health”: the phrase is repeated so often that it no longer says anything. Good by how much, for whom, and how do we know? In a check-up, you are weighed, your blood pressure is taken, your blood is looked at. What your heart, lungs and muscles produce when you push hard is almost never measured. This capacity is called cardiorespiratory fitness. Its reference measure is VO2max: the maximum amount of oxygen your body can consume in one minute, relative to your weight.11

In 2016, the American Heart Association called for this fitness to be measured routinely, like blood pressure, and noted that it is absent from the common risk calculators.12,13 That does not yet answer your question, which has two parts.

The first part is an observation. Does a person's endurance level tell us about their lifespan, beyond what age, weight, smoking and blood pressure already say? The second is more demanding. If so, is it because endurance protects, or because it reflects something else: good health to begin with, favourable genes, a healthier lifestyle? In the first case, measuring your endurance tells you where you stand. In the second, working on it is a lever on your trajectory. These are not the same conclusions, and you cannot move from one to the other without evidence.

The question

Does your endurance level predict how long you will live, and does improving your endurance change that length of life, or is endurance only the reflection of something else?

We proceed in six steps, from the general to the specific: the whole population, the studies that cross-check each other, the shape of the relationship, what VO2max measures, the comparison with other factors, then the most serious objections. The answer comes after that.

What is at stake

What is at stake is not abstract. First there is health in the sense of disease: the studies we are about to read link cardiorespiratory fitness to mortality, to cardiovascular events and to heart failure. The authors of a large recent overview also link it to a lower risk of depression and dementia, which they themselves present as an association.7

Then there is independence. Without training, VO2max falls by about 1% a year (0.4 to 0.5 mL/kg/min), faster after age 70.11 The lower your starting point at 40, the less margin you have at 70: this is reasoning, not a study result.

There is lifespan itself, which studies measure most solidly, because a death is not open to debate. There is performance: VO2max determines the intensity of effort you can sustain for a long time. And there is a decision at stake. If endurance is only a marker, a poor score is just a signal. If it is a lever, ignoring it is a missed opportunity, especially for those starting from a low level. Being wrong in either direction costs time, energy or years: the question cannot be left unanswered.

Step 1 of 6 · The whole population

In a large cohort, the higher the fitness, the fewer deaths

We start with the largest study available, because it gives the order of magnitude. Researchers at the Cleveland Clinic went back over the records of 122,007 patients who took a treadmill exercise test between 1991 and 2014. The mean age was 53.4 years, 59.2% were men, and 13,637 of them (11.2%) died during a median follow-up of 8.4 years.1,2

Each patient was placed in one of five levels, according to their treadmill performance compared with that of people of the same age and sex: low (below the 25th percentile), below average, above average, high, elite (97.7th percentile and above). The ranking is therefore relative: an “elite” patient at 70 does not have the absolute performance of an “elite” patient at 30.1,3

The higher the fitness level, the lower the risk of death

Levels defined by percentile according to age and sex. Heights calculated as the inverse of the published adjusted risk ratios (1/1.95, 1/2.75, 1/3.90, 1/5.04), and therefore approximate. Source: Mandsager et al., JAMA Network Open, 2018.1,2

What this means

The risk falls at every level, with no plateau where it stops. Between the lowest level and elite, the risk of death is about five times lower (adjusted risk ratio of 5.04, i.e. 80% lower for elite). These calculations take into account age, sex, weight, smoking, diabetes, hypertension and cardiac history, among other things.1

These patients were referred for an exercise test at a single centre, and their levels are estimated from the speed and incline of the treadmill. It is an observational study: it shows that two things go together, not which one drives the other.1,2 We will come back to this at the last step.

It remains to be seen whether the same signal appears when the population, the era and the method change.

Step 2 of 6 · The studies that cross-check each other

The same signal appears across very different populations and methods

Three other sources allow us to check. The first is a cohort of 6,213 men referred for an exercise test, followed for 6.2 years on average, with 1,256 deaths. Each additional MET (the MET is the unit that expresses effort as multiples of resting expenditure, one MET being about 3.5 mL/kg/min) was accompanied by a 12% improvement in survival.4,11 Above all, the authors separated men with no known disease (2,534) from those with cardiovascular disease or an abnormal test (3,679). In both groups, the least fit fifth had a risk of death 4.5 times and 4.1 times higher than the fittest fifth.4

The second is a meta-analysis of 33 studies covering 102,980 healthy adults and 6,910 deaths. It finds a risk of death 1.70 times higher in those with low fitness (under 7.9 METs) than in those with high fitness (10.9 METs or more), and 1.40 times higher than in those at an intermediate level. For each additional MET, the risk of death is multiplied by 0.87, i.e. 13% lower.5

The third is the most recent: a summary of 26 systematic reviews, i.e. 199 cohorts and more than 20.9 million observations. In the general population, the risk of death of very fit people is 0.47 times that of people with low fitness (interval 0.39 to 0.56). For each additional MET, the risk is 11 to 17% lower depending on the meta-analyses. For heart failure, the ratio between high and low fitness is 0.31.6

In every study, one more MET goes with a lower risk of death

Risk ratio of death per additional MET, with 95% confidence interval. A value below 1 means a lower risk. The two Lang estimates come from two different meta-analyses in the overview. Sources: Kodama 2009, Lang 2024, Myers 2002.4,5,6

What this means

When a relationship reappears in men tested in a clinic, in healthy adults and in dozens of cohorts, it is unlikely to come from a flaw specific to a single study. Three more METs would correspond, extending Kodama's average effect, to a risk about a third lower (0.87 to the power of 3 gives 0.66). This last figure is a derived calculation, not a measured result, and it assumes that the effect accumulates steadily.

There is an important reservation, which the authors of the 2024 overview give themselves: the certainty of evidence, assessed with the GRADE framework, ranges from very low to moderate depending on the outcome.6 These studies are observational and define “low” and “high” fitness differently: we can conclude that the relationship is consistent, not what its exact size is.

If the relationship is consistent, its shape remains to be established. Is a gain spread across the whole scale, or concentrated at one specific point? The answer determines what you should aim for.

Step 3 of 6 · The shape of the relationship

The biggest gain lies at the exit from the lowest level, and the benefit does not stop abruptly afterwards

In the Cleveland Clinic study, we can calculate how much the risk falls at each step, starting from the published risk ratios (1.95; 2.75; 3.90; 5.04 for the low group compared with the other four).2

Each step up in fitness lowers the risk, the first the most

Relative drop in risk of death when moving from one level to the next. Figures derived from the adjusted risk ratios of Mandsager et al. (1.95; 2.75; 3.90; 5.04), rounded. Source: JAMA Network Open, 2018.2

What this means

The first step is the highest: going from the least fit quarter to the level just above lowers the risk by about half. The following steps are each worth about 29%, then the last 23%. Every step remains useful, but leaving the bottom pays the most. If you start from a low level, you do not need to aim for the elite level to get most of the benefit. A cardiologist who was not involved in the study sums it up like this: the gap between neighbouring levels is modest, and the biggest gain is at the exit from the lowest level.3

These percentages are relative and derived from the published risk ratios: they do not tell you how many deaths are avoided.

That leaves the top end of the scale. Is there a level beyond which more endurance is of no use, or even harmful? In the Cleveland Clinic study, the elite group has a risk 0.77 times that of the high group (interval 0.63 to 0.95), and 0.71 in people over 70 (0.52 to 0.98). But the elite group counts only 93 deaths, and the advantage is not significant separately in men or in women.1,2 A much larger cohort, of 750,302 American veterans aged 30 to 95, with 174,807 deaths over a median follow-up of 10.2 years, finds the lowest risk around 14 METs, with the least fit group at about 4 times the risk of the extremely fit group (4.09). Its authors do not report any rise in risk at extreme levels. It includes 110,637 people in their seventies and 45,232 women.8

What this means

No clear ceiling in the data we read: the risk keeps falling or levels off, and no study we read shows that being very fit increases mortality. But the advantage of elite over the level just below is the least well established, as it rests on few deaths. For a reader who is not an athlete, the practical message is that of the bottom step.

We now know that the link exists, that it is consistent and graded. To judge whether it can be causal, we need to understand exactly what this measure captures.

Step 4 of 6 · The mechanism

VO2max sums up the work of the heart, the vessels and the muscles

VO2max is the product of two things: the flow of blood your heart can send out at maximal effort (cardiac output), and the amount of oxygen your muscles extract from that blood. This is the Fick equation. In most people at sea level, it is maximal cardiac output that is limiting, at 5 to 6 litres of blood per minute for each litre of oxygen consumed. On the muscle side, extraction depends on capillaries and mitochondria, the structures that use oxygen.11

What training changes is specific. It does not raise maximum heart rate. It increases the volume of blood ejected with each beat, thanks to a physiological enlargement of the heart's chamber, and it lowers heart rate at rest and at moderate effort. Maximal cardiac output can thus rise to at least five times the resting value, more in the best athletes.11

What this means

VO2max is not the measure of one organ. It is a measure of the whole chain: pump, circulation, muscle. That is what makes it plausible as a general indicator: a weak link somewhere shows up at maximal effort. And it is also what explains the ambiguity of the number: a low VO2max can come from a lack of training, an excess of fat mass, a disease that is setting in, or genes. A plausible mechanism is not proof that raising the number lengthens life.

The mechanism also explains why a field test is an estimate. A meta-analysis of 57 studies finds that the 20-metre shuttle run test is correlated at 0.66 to 0.84 with VO2max measured in the laboratory. Its authors specify that the score remains an estimate and not a direct measurement.19 What is true of VO2max is therefore also true of your score: it describes a capacity, with a margin of error.

If endurance is a good indicator of the state of the whole chain, the next question is how it compares with the risk factors we already monitor.

Step 5 of 6 · The comparison with other factors

Endurance carries as much weight as the risk factors everyone knows

The phrase “best predictor” comes from comparisons of this kind. In a study by Blair and colleagues of 25,341 men and 7,080 women who had a preventive check-up with an exercise test (601 and 89 deaths), the researchers compared the weight of low fitness (the least fit fifth) with that of other predictors.9

Being unfit weighs in the same range as smoking

Adjusted relative risks of all-cause death. Blair et al., JAMA, 1996. The cholesterol and systolic pressure values are not included (identical values in the abstract, to be checked).9

What this means

In men as in women, being unfit multiplies the risk by amounts close to those for smoking (1.52 against 1.65 in men, 2.10 against 1.99 in women). In the same study, fit people who smoked or had high blood pressure or cholesterol had lower adjusted death rates than unfit people with none of these factors.9 It compares groups: it does not say that smoking becomes safe when you are fit.

Other studies give varying orders of magnitude, which is normal: it all depends on what is being compared. In the Cleveland Clinic cohort, the risk ratio is 1.41 for smoking, 1.40 for diabetes and 1.29 for coronary artery disease. A single extra fitness level (from the below-average level to the above-average level) gives the same 1.41 as smoking, but the gap between the two extremes, 5.04, has no equivalent in this list.1,2 In Myers's cohort, among men with no known disease, exercise capacity is the strongest predictor, smoking comes next, and hypertension and diabetes are not significant.4 “Best predictor” is therefore too strong: depending on the study and the contrast chosen, endurance weighs as much as smoking or much more. It is safe to say that it is one of the most powerful predictors.

A comparison also brings a useful nuance about weight. A meta-analysis of ten studies in which fitness is measured objectively concludes that unfit people have about twice the risk of death of fit people of normal weight, whatever their body mass index, and that fit people who are overweight or obese have a risk comparable to that of fit people of normal weight.10

All these results remain associations. The last step is to put them to the test: what happens when we actively look for the opposite explanation?

Step 6 of 6 · The objections

What holds up when we try to tear the result down, and what remains uncertain

This is the step that decides what we can claim. Four serious objections arise, and each has a partial answer.

Objection 1: fit people are simply healthier to begin with

This is reverse causation. A person who is ill, sometimes without knowing it, performs less well in exercise. Their illness then explains both the poor score and the death to come. The authors of the Cleveland Clinic study acknowledge that their design cannot decide between fitness that protects and fitness that reflects better health.2 The gap nevertheless persists after adjustment for known diseases, and in Myers's men it exists both without known disease and with it.1,4 This does not remove the possibility of an undetected disease.

Objection 2: what if we look at the same people over time?

One study repeated the test in the same men, an average of 4.9 years apart: 9,777 men, then followed for 5.1 years, with 223 deaths.14 Comparing each man with himself rules out stable traits specific to each person.

Men who improve die less than those who stay unfit

All-cause death rates, age-adjusted, per 10,000 man-years. 9,777 men from a preventive clinic, 223 deaths. Source: Blair et al., JAMA, 1995 (abstract of the article).14

What this means

Men who moved from unfit to fit have a risk of death 44% lower than men who stayed unfit (interval 25 to 59%).14 This is the closest thing to an effect of change. But those who improve may also change other habits or have been healthier to begin with, and this is not a trial in which training was assigned by lot.

Objection 3: it is the genes

Part of cardiorespiratory fitness is hereditary. A cardiologist quoted in the specialist press estimates it at 15 to 30%, an expert's figure and not a result we read in a publication.3 If genes favour both high fitness and a long life, the observed relationship could be misleading. Two studies test this idea, and neither dismisses it.

The first follows Finnish twins: 11,325 people, including 4,190 complete pairs. It concerns self-reported vigorous physical activity, not measured fitness. Persistent vigorous activity is associated with a risk of death of 0.73 (0.61 to 0.88) after adjustment. Among dizygotic twins where one is active and the other is not, the ratio is 0.58 (0.39 to 0.88). Among identical twins where one is active and the other is not, it is 1.00 (0.52 to 1.94), but only 34 pairs of identical twins are in this situation, and the interval is wide: the result is too imprecise to conclude.15

The second is a Mendelian randomisation study, which uses genetic variants as a substitute for a natural “experiment”. It concerns an estimated VO2max in about 70,783 UK Biobank participants and the longevity of their parents (about 1.01 million parents). It finds no causal association between VO2max and longevity, even though endurance is a strong predictor in observational studies. On the other hand, fat mass and type 2 diabetes each have an independent causal effect on longevity. The authors conclude that VO2max is more likely a consequence of body composition and activity than a cause.16

What this means

This is the result that qualifies the usual headline the most. It is possible that the VO2max figure is mostly a thermometer: it measures the cumulative effect of a lifestyle, a weight and an activity level, rather than an isolated lever. This study has its limits (VO2max estimated with a submaximal test, longevity measured by the survival of parents) and does not settle the question either, but it rules out presenting VO2max as a proven cause.

Objection 4: has training been tested at random against mortality?

Yes, once, and the answer is disappointing. In the Generation 100 trial in Norway, 1,567 people aged 70 to 77 were randomly assigned to three groups: high-intensity intervals (two sessions a week at about 90% of maximum heart rate), moderate continuous training (about 70%), or the activity recommended by the authorities. After five years, mortality in the reference group was 4.7%.17

The randomised trial on mortality does not settle it

All-cause death risk ratios at 5 years, with 95% confidence interval, logarithmic scale. 1,567 people aged 70 to 77. Source: Stensvold et al., Generation 100, BMJ, 2020 (abstract).17

What this means

None of the three comparisons is statistically significant: each interval contains 1. The authors conclude that combining the two types of training does not change mortality compared with recommended activity, with a trend towards lower mortality for high-intensity intervals that cannot be confirmed. The trial compares supervised training with an activity guideline already followed by most people (80% of participants had a moderate or high activity level at baseline), with few deaths. It does not compare training with no activity: it provides neither evidence of a benefit on mortality, nor evidence of no benefit.

And is improvement itself possible?

On this point, we have randomised trials, and they answer clearly. A meta-analysis of 53 trials in 1,514 adults compares interval training with no training: VO2max gains on average 5.45 mL/kg/min in healthy adults, 3.54 in overweight or obese adults and 1.71 in athletes. The authors point to strong heterogeneity and a risk of publication bias.18 Gains vary with the population: smaller in athletes, who are already highly trained, than in healthy adults, and smaller in overweight adults than in healthy ones. So there is no simple rule of the “the lower you start, the more you gain” type.

The answer to the problem

We had posed two questions. Here are the answers, with their degree of certainty.

Does your endurance say anything about your lifespan? Yes, and it is solid. The relationship appears in a cohort of 122,007 patients, in men with no known disease, in a meta-analysis of 33 studies, in a summary of 199 cohorts and in 750,302 veterans. It is graded, it persists after adjustment for known factors, and it is of the same order as smoking in several studies. The clearest relative gain lies at the exit from the lowest level. This is the best-established part, even if the 2024 overview notes that the certainty of evidence ranges from very low to moderate depending on the outcome.

Does improving your endurance change that lifespan? It is probable, but not demonstrated. For: the gap is consistent, it exists without known disease, those who improve have a lower risk than those who stay unfit, and the mechanism is plausible. Pending: a genetic study finds no causal link between VO2max and longevity, identical twins do not allow a conclusion, and the only randomised trial on mortality found nothing. The most honest summary: endurance is a powerful marker, its causal link with lifespan is not proven, and part of that link probably runs through what builds it, that is, activity, weight and general health.

Established on another level: training raises VO2max, with very variable gains depending on the population. And measuring your endurance has a value of its own, even without settling causality: a low score is a signal, and a rising score shows that what you are doing is having an effect.

What to put in place

The following actions are ordered, and each builds on what precedes it. The retest frequency is an editorial choice based on the length of these protocols (4 to 12 weeks) and on the noise in the tests, not a figure from a study.

  1. Measure your level with the endurance test on this page.A field test gives an estimate with a margin of error, not your exact VO2max.19 It places you against age and sex reference values, as the five levels in the studies do. It estimates, it does not diagnose.
  2. If you are in the lowest level, aim first to leave it.This is where the drop in risk is largest in the data (step 3). According to the cardiologist quoted above, following the activity recommendations, i.e. 150 minutes a week of moderate intensity or 75 minutes of vigorous intensity, may be enough to leave this level.3
  3. Progress in blocks of a few weeks.In the meta-analysis, the interval protocols that do better than moderate continuous training last 4 to 12 weeks.18 The lower your starting point, the more you can expect to gain. No data we read allows us to say that a particular intensity reduces mortality: the Generation 100 trial does not settle it.17
  4. Retest every 8 to 12 weeks, under the same conditions.Same surface, same time of day, same warm-up. For the Cooper test, the variation from one attempt to the next is about 52 metres in runners: below that, a difference proves nothing about your training.20 Once a year is enough to monitor the age-related slope.
  5. Do not replace everything else.The genetic study finds an independent causal effect of fat mass and type 2 diabetes on longevity. Endurance adds to blood pressure, weight and smoking, it does not replace them.

A very low score, chest pain or abnormal breathlessness call for medical advice before you train harder.

What these figures do not say
  • The patients in the main study were referred for an exercise test at a single centre, and several cohorts are exclusively or mostly male.1,4,9
  • All the relationships with mortality come from observational studies. An undetected disease can explain both a poor score and a death.2
  • No randomised trial we read shows that a gain in VO2max reduces mortality by a specific amount.

Frequently asked questions

Should you aim for the elite level?

The data do not require it. The clearest gain is between the lowest level and the next, and the advantage of elite is not demonstrated in all subgroups.2,3

Is my field test score my VO2max?

No. It is an estimate, useful mainly for tracking your progress under the same conditions.12,19

Is a poor score permanent?

Nothing in these studies suggests so: training raises VO2max in all the populations studied, with larger or smaller gains.18
